title.en: History: Social and Religious Reform Movements in the 19th Century

text.en: Meena learnt about a reformer who ended a cruel custom in India. "Raja Ram Mohan Roy," said her teacher.

In the nineteenth century, social and religious reformers worked to end evil customs. Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj and fought sati, which was banned in 1829. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar worked for widow remarriage.
Dayananda Saraswati started the Arya Samaj and Ramakrishna and Vivekananda spread the message of service. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan promoted modern education among Muslims at Aligarh. Jyotiba Phule fought caste discrimination.
In Tamil Nadu, Vallalar Ramalinga Adigal taught compassion, Iyothee Thass worked for the oppressed, and Muthulakshmi Reddy and others worked for women. The reforms led to laws and a new social awakening.

In early nineteenth-century India, printing presses, English education and debates over ancient texts inspired thinkers to challenge rigid caste rules, child marriage and illiteracy.
Pioneer Raja Ram Mohan Roy, called the Father of the Indian Renaissance, used Sanskrit, Persian and English scholarship to oppose idol worship, sati and polygamy.

board.text: Raja Ram Mohan Roy: Indian Renaissance

text.en: His Brahmo Samaj (1828) championed monotheism, women's property rights and modern science, helping Governor-General William Bentinck outlaw sati in 1829.
After him, Debendranath Tagore and Keshab Chandra Sen kept Brahmo Samaj alive, while Henry Vivian Derozio's Young Bengal sparked fearless rational questioning.
In Bengal, scholar Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar proved from sacred texts that widow remarriage was lawful, leading to the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 and opening girls' schools.
In western India, Prarthana Samaj—led by M.G. Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar—worked for inter-caste dining, widow remarriage and raising marriage age.
Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded Arya Samaj in 1875 with the slogan 'Go Back to the Vedas', opposing caste by birth and founding Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) schools.
Ramakrishna Paramahamsa taught that all sincere faiths lead to the same truth, and his disciple Swami Vivekananda carried Vedanta to the 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions.
Founding the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897, Vivekananda urged youth to serve the poor—'daridra narayana'—combining spiritual confidence with practical schools and hospitals.
Meanwhile, Annie Besant led the Theosophical Society from Adyar in Madras, reviving pride in Indian philosophy and founding Central Hindu College at Benares.
Most inspiringly, anti-caste pioneers attacked untouchability head-on: Jyotiba Phule and Savitribai Phule opened India's first modern girls' school in Pune (1848) and Satyashodhak Samaj (1873).

board.text: Jyotiba & Savitribai Phule fight caste & open schools

text.en: Phule's book Gulamgiri ('Slavery') exposed caste oppression, while Narayana Guru in Kerala proclaimed 'One Caste, One Religion, One God for All Humankind'.
In Kerala too, Ayyankali founded Sadhu Jana Paripalana Sangam, winning school entry and equal road rights for Dalit families.

board.text: Ayyankali wins school & public rights in Kerala

text.en: Among Muslims, Sir Syed Ahmad Khan launched the Aligarh Movement (1875), blending Urdu and science education to modernise community life.

board.text: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan & Aligarh Movement

text.en: Among Parsis, Reformers including Dadabhai Naoroji founded Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha, while Sikh Singh Sabha and Akali reformers protected gurudwaras and promoted Punjabi schools.
Look closely at Tamil Nadu! Saint Vallalar Ramalinga Adigal founded Samarasa Vedha Sanmarga Sangam in 1865 and built the Dharmasalai at Vadalur so no hungry person goes unfed.
Even today his eternal flame at Vadalur symbolises Jeevakarunya—loving kindness to all living creatures beyond caste or creed.

board.text: Vallalar's Vadalur kitchen feeds all even today

text.en: In Madras, Pandit Iyothee Thass ran 'Oru Paisa Tamilan', revived Siddha and egalitarian Tamil heritage, and championed oppressed communities long before independence.
In southern Tamil Nadu too, Vaikunda Swamigal preached Samathuva Samajam—equality without caste prejudice or temple exploitation.
Notice the twin styles: reform movements like Brahmo Samaj updated society from within, while revival movements like Arya Samaj drew strength from ancient roots.
Trace the legacy: printing & education -> courageous reformers -> new laws (1829, 1856) + anti-caste awakening -> democratic, equal India.
From Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Phule to Vallalar and Iyothee Thass, nineteenth-century reformers proved that compassion and justice build a free nation.

board.text: Compassion & reason laid India's modern base

problem.en: Compare how Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Jyotiba Phule and Vallalar each tackled inequality in 19th-century India.

text.en: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (Bengal).

why.en: Fought women's oppression—especially sati—using reasoned debate, newspapers and law reform (1829 Act).

text.en: Jyotiba & Savitribai Phule (Maharashtra).

why.en: Challenged caste hierarchy from below by opening girls' and lower-caste schools and founding Satyashodhak Samaj.

text.en: Vallalar Ramalinga Adigal (Tamil Nadu).

why.en: Taught Jeevakarunya (universal compassion) and started free food kitchens at Vadalur for all people without caste barriers.

prompt.en: A friend says Vivekananda founded the Brahmo Samaj. How will you reply?
